citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
The licensee is not using appropriate methods to prevent and treat disease and illness in 2 adult dogs.
One adult female Yorkshire Terrier identified as “Poppy” has areas of thinning hair coat and visible fleas. The licensee is
currently using only dawn dish soap for flea prevention. “Poppy” also has a build up of brown organic material present on
approximately 50% of the upper cheek teeth. The right side upper cheek teeth are fully encased in hardened medium
brown plaque material.
One adult female Pug identified as “Heaven” has a widespread area of skin on her abdomen surrounding all mammary
glands that is reddened and inflamed with areas that are moist and oozing. The licensee is currently treating the area with
topical antibiotic ointment.
Not using appropriate methods to control parasites like fleas can cause skin irritation and discomfort and can progress to
more severe disease. Poor dental health can cause pain and suffering. Skin conditions that are not appropriately treated
can be painful and progress to more severe disease.
The facility must use appropriate methods to prevent, control, diagnose, and treat diseases and injuries in the regulated
animals. The facility must ensure each animal receives adequate veterinary care at all times. The facility must have this
dog evaluated by a licensed veterinarian to assess their health to develop an effective treatment plan. These medical
records must be available for APHIS inspection.
To be corrected by: 5:00 PM 29-June-2026

Several dogs did not have water. Inspectors asked the licensee to provide the following dogs with a bowl of water. When
provided with water one young adult Rottweiler drank for over 2 minutes from a bowl and before that was licking water
from a dripping hose for ~30 seconds. A young adult pug drank leisurely for approximately 10 seconds. One adult French
Bulldog did not drink once offered water. One adult French Bulldog drank continuously for 50 seconds. One adult yorkie
female with three puppies drank continuously for 45 seconds.
Dogs that do not have access to water may become dehydrated and reduced water consumption may lead to additional
medical problems. Potable water must be continuously available for the health and well-being of the dogs, unless
restricted by the attending veterinarian.
To be corrected by: 26-June-2026

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
Several enclosures housing adult dogs and puppies have not had excreta removed daily and several animals did not have
a clean, dry place in their enclosures.
*One sheltered building had two enclosures housing a total of 3 adult Rottweilers. The licensee was cleaning one
enclosure’s outdoor run with a hose when inspectors arrived. The other enclosure had a wet accumulation of feces, and
the hose water was spraying feces into this enclosure. The indoor portion of these enclosures being hosed had damp
wood shavings and fecal material. The dogs were not removed from the enclosures and could not remain clean and dry
while the enclosure was being cleaned. The dogs were wet in appearance.
*One indoor enclosure housing two adult yorkies had several days’ worth of fecal material with white mold present on the
feces in the corner.
*Two indoor enclosures housing two French Bulldogs had an accumulation of several days’ worth of feces and the dogs
did not have any clean floor space.
*Two indoor enclosures housing 2 dams with litters of puppies (10 puppies total) had an accumulation of several days’
worth of feces and the dogs did not have any clean floor space. Additionally, one female adult Pug had a skin condition
likely brought on by the exposure to fecal material. The skin on her stomach was reddened with moisture and oozing
organic material.
Failure to remove excreta daily from primary enclosures is resulting in an accumulation of feces and leading to an
increased risk of disease hazards, odors, possible discomfort and medical ailments to the animals.
Excreta and food waste must be removed from primary enclosures daily, and from under primary enclosures as often as
necessary to prevent an excessive accumulation of feces and food waste, to prevent soiling of the dogs or cats contained
in the primary enclosures, and to reduce disease hazards, insects, pests and odors.
To be corrected by: 27-June-2026
A complete routine inspection was conducted on 26-June-2026. This inspection report is limited to the direct non-
compliances and the veterinary care non-compliance identified during that inspection. An additional inspection report will
be delivered with the other issues identified during this inspection.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with the licensee.
Additional Inspectors:
Paige Johnson, ANIMAL CARE INSPECTOR n
